sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About HAIC-FOLFOX for Advanced HCC with Portal Vein Thrombus
sectionToMerge.intro: Hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) with the FOLFOX regimen has become a widely used approach in China for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), especially when a tumor thrombus is present in the portal vein. These answers explain how it works, who it may suit, and what international patients should know.

items.q: What is HAIC-FOLFOX for liver cancer?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX is hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy that delivers the FOLFOX drug combination (oxaliplatin, fluorouracil, and leucovorin) directly into the liver artery feeding the tumor. Because the chemotherapy is infused close to the cancer, tumor tissue is exposed to high drug concentrations while the rest of the body receives less. It is used mainly for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and is delivered over several treatment cycles under specialist supervision.

items.q: How is HAIC different from TACE?
items.a: HAIC delivers chemotherapy as a prolonged infusion into the hepatic artery, while TACE (transarterial chemoembolization) combines chemotherapy with particles that block the tumor's blood supply. HAIC does not rely on embolization, which may make it more suitable for large tumors or when a portal vein tumor thrombus limits blood flow. The choice between them depends on tumor size, spread, liver function, and specialist assessment, and should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is a portal vein tumor thrombus in HCC?
items.a: A portal vein tumor thrombus is an extension of liver cancer into the portal vein, the main vessel carrying blood to the liver. It is a sign of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and can make some treatments, such as surgery or standard TACE, more difficult or unsafe. HAIC-FOLFOX is often considered in these cases because it can target tumors even when portal vein involvement is present, though suitability always depends on specialist review.

items.q: Why is HAIC-FOLFOX widely used in China?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX has become a preferred option in many Chinese liver cancer centers because clinical experience there suggests it may help control advanced HCC, including tumors with portal vein thrombus. Several studies from China have explored its use alone or combined with targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Availability and clinical practice vary by country, and whether this approach is appropriate for a specific patient should be confirmed by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: Who may be eligible for HAIC-FOLFOX?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX may be considered for selected patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly larger tumors or those with portal vein tumor thrombus that are not suitable for surgery. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, liver function, overall health, previous treatment, and specialist review. Patients generally need adequate liver reserve and a treatable arterial route. Final decisions on suitability should always be made by the treating medical team after full assessment.

HAIC-FOLFOX is given through a thin catheter placed into the hepatic artery, usually via a small groin puncture guided by imaging. The FOLFOX drugs are then infused slowly over many hours, often across two to three days per cycle. Treatment is typically repeated every few weeks for several cycles, with response checked by scans. The exact schedule is planned and adjusted by the treating oncology and interventional team.

items.q: How many cycles of HAIC-FOLFOX are usually needed?
items.a: The number of HAIC-FOLFOX cycles varies for each patient and is decided by the treating team based on tumor response and tolerance. Many treatment protocols involve several cycles, often repeated every three to four weeks, with imaging used to assess progress. Some patients receive additional targeted therapy or immunotherapy alongside HAIC. The plan can change depending on how the tumor responds and how well the patient handles treatment, so individual guidance is essential.

items.q: What are the possible side effects of HAIC-FOLFOX?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX can cause side effects such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, reduced blood counts, and temporary liver enzyme changes. Oxaliplatin may cause nerve-related tingling, and there are risks linked to the catheter procedure itself, including bleeding or vessel injury. Most effects are managed with supportive care, but severity varies between patients. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported promptly to the treating medical team.

items.q: Is HAIC-FOLFOX a cure for advanced liver cancer?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX is not a guaranteed cure for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma; it is used to try to control the tumor, shrink it, or slow its progression. In some patients, good response may make other treatments, such as surgery, possible later, but outcomes vary widely. Results depend on tumor stage, liver function, portal vein involvement, and overall health. Realistic goals and expected benefits should be discussed openly with the treating oncology team.

items.q: How much does HAIC-FOLFOX treatment cost?
items.a: The cost of HAIC-FOLFOX varies widely and cannot be quoted as a fixed figure. Final cost depends on the hospital, country, diagnosis, tumor stage, number of cycles, additional drugs such as targeted therapy or immunotherapy, imaging, hospital stay, and any complications. Prices may differ significantly between centers. A personalized estimate can only be given after medical review, and patients should confirm all charges directly with the treating hospital.

items.q: Which countries offer HAIC-FOLFOX for HCC?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX is used most extensively in China and some other parts of Asia, where it features prominently in liver cancer treatment practice. Availability in other countries varies, as not all centers offer hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy. Access depends on local expertise, equipment, and clinical guidelines. Patients interested in this treatment should confirm availability with individual hospitals and discuss whether it is an appropriate option with their treating oncology team.

Availability of HAIC-FOLFOX in India varies by hospital and depends on whether a center has the interventional radiology expertise and infusion protocols required. It is not as widely established as in China, though some specialized liver cancer centers may offer hepatic arterial infusion approaches. Patients should confirm availability directly with individual hospitals. Whether this treatment suits a particular case should be assessed by a qualified oncology team after reviewing medical records.

items.q: Can HAIC-FOLFOX be combined with targeted therapy or immunotherapy?
items.a: HAIC-FOLFOX is sometimes combined with targeted therapy, such as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or with immunotherapy in selected patients with advanced HCC. Several studies from China have explored these combinations to try to improve tumor control. Whether a combination is appropriate depends on tumor characteristics, liver function, biomarker profile, previous treatment, and overall health. Any combined approach should be planned and monitored closely by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for HAIC-FOLFOX in liver cancer?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study HAIC-FOLFOX for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, often testing it alongside targeted therapy or immunotherapy. Trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, and enrollment is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Taking part does not guarantee benefit. Patients interested in a trial should discuss eligibility with their oncology team and review the specific requirements of each study before making a decision.

items.q: What happens if HAIC-FOLFOX does not work?
items.a: If HAIC-FOLFOX does not control the tumor, the treating team may consider other options depending on the situation. These can include changing systemic therapy, adding targeted therapy or immunotherapy, exploring clinical trials, or focusing on symptom control and quality of life. The next step depends on tumor response, liver function, overall health, and patient preferences. Ongoing scans and specialist review help guide any change in the treatment plan.

items.q: Can HAIC-FOLFOX help downstage a tumor for surgery?
items.a: In some selected patients, HAIC-FOLFOX may shrink an advanced liver tumor enough to be reconsidered for surgery or other curative-intent treatment, a process sometimes called downstaging. This outcome is not guaranteed and depends on how the tumor responds, liver function, and portal vein involvement. Any decision to proceed with surgery afterward requires careful reassessment by the treating surgical and oncology team and cannot be assumed in advance.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to assess HAIC-FOLFOX suitability?
items.a: To assess whether HAIC-FOLFOX may be suitable, specialists usually need recent imaging such as CT or MRI of the liver, blood tests including liver function and tumor markers like AFP, pathology or biopsy reports if available, and a summary of previous treatments. Details of overall health and other medical conditions are also important. A complete and up-to-date set of records helps the treating oncology team give accurate, personalized guidance.

items.q: What should international patients know before traveling for HAIC-FOLFOX?
items.a: International patients should understand that access to HAIC-FOLFOX abroad depends on hospital acceptance, medical record review, visa approval, travel fitness, and overall condition, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Because treatment involves several cycles over weeks, patients should plan for an extended stay, follow-up scans, and possible additional therapy. Arrangements for a second opinion, cost estimate, and follow-up care at home should also be considered before traveling.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with HAIC-FOLFOX?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to make the process clearer for patients and caregivers, without replacing the guidance of doctors or hospitals.
